## Warm-up retrieval

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. What does a confidence interval for a regression slope $\beta_1$ tell you?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The probability that the slope is positive</li>
  <li>A range of plausible values for the *population* slope, based on the sample</li>
  <li>The exact value of the slope</li>
  <li>The R-squared of the model</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Same logic as a CI for a mean: a range likely to contain the true population value, given the sample data.</div>
:::


## What you'll be able to do

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Apply the full data-science pipeline (import → wrangle → visualize → model) to a multi-step case study
- Diagnose and address common data quality issues (skewness, missing values, outliers)
- Build a regression model that captures interaction between variables
- Communicate statistical findings clearly to a non-technical audience

::: {.predict}
Before we begin: which of these objectives feels least familiar to you right now? Hold that in mind — we'll check back at the end.
:::

<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. When a numerical variable is *right-skewed* (a long right tail), a useful transformation often is:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Subtracting the mean</li>
  <li>Squaring the values</li>
  <li>Taking the logarithm (`log10()`)</li>
  <li>Multiplying by 10</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> Log transformation compresses large values relative to small ones, often producing a more symmetric distribution that's easier to model.</div>
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q2. What's the most important reason to communicate uncertainty (e.g., confidence intervals) along with point estimates in a data story?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>To make the report longer</li>
  <li>To accurately represent how much the estimate could vary across samples</li>
  <li>To impress the reader with statistical jargon</li>
  <li>To meet a regulatory requirement</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Reporting only point estimates implies more precision than the data supports. CIs (or other uncertainty measures) honestly communicate sampling variability.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Concluding remarks

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q4. A right-skewed variable like house prices is log10-transformed. After fitting `lm(log10_price ~ log10_size)`, the slope is 0.5. The interpretation:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>For every 1-square-foot increase in size, log10(price) increases by 0.5</li>
  <li>**For every 10× increase in size, log10(price) increases by 0.5 — i.e., price multiplies by $10^{0.5} \approx 3.16$**</li>
  <li>Price increases by 50%</li>
  <li>The relationship cannot be interpreted</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> With *both* variables on a log scale, slopes describe **multiplicative** changes: a 10× increase in $x$ predicts a $10^{\beta}$× change in $y$. This is the elasticity interpretation common in economics.</div>
:::
